I have searched and fetched the key commentary pages available. Here are the verse-by-verse notes, organized as requested.

## Genesis 47 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1
Joseph went and told Pharaoh that his father and brothers had arrived from Canaan with all their possessions and were now in Goshen.

- **Gill** notes that Joseph first went alone to Pharaoh's court, not wanting his family's arrival to appear secretive. He mentions flocks and herds to show they were not beggars and to secure proper pasturage. They halted in Goshen awaiting further direction from Pharaoh. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)
- **Ellicott** observes that though Joseph had long wished Goshen to be their dwelling-place, it was necessary to obtain Pharaoh's permission; at this point Joseph only mentions that they had halted there. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Joseph "went up to the royal presence" as he had proposed in Genesis 46:31, telling Pharaoh that his family had arrived as Pharaoh himself had desired (Genesis 45:17–18). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: When Joseph spoke these words, it was the fulfillment of both God's plan and Joseph's personal desire — he was again with his father and brothers. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)

### v. 2
Joseph chose five of his brothers and presented them before Pharaoh.

- **Gill**: The Hebrew word for "some" literally means "the extremity," leading to various rabbinic theories — that Joseph chose the weakest (lest Pharaoh make them soldiers), or the strongest (to make a good impression), or both young and old. Gill himself holds that Joseph made no calculated choice but simply took five who were at hand. The Targum of Jonathan names them as Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher; Jarchi suggests Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Issachar, and Benjamin — but Gill says no reliance can be placed on these traditions. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)
- **Ellicott**: The number "five" appears repeatedly in the Joseph narrative (Genesis 43:34; 45:22) and may have held special significance among Egyptians, as the number seven did among the Jews. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The phrase "from the end of his brethren" means from the whole body of his brethren (contra the rabbinic theories), and he took five men. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)

### v. 3
Pharaoh asked the brothers their occupation. They answered, "Your servants are shepherds, both we and our fathers."

- **Ellicott**: Joseph had instructed them to add "and our fathers" (Genesis 46:34) because occupations were hereditary among Egyptians; Pharaoh would conclude that in their case also no change in their mode of life was possible. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Gill**: This was the very question Joseph had told them would be asked (Genesis 46:33). It was probably Pharaoh's usual question for those seeking to settle in his dominions, ensuring there were no idle vagrants. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary** notes the brothers answered exactly as Joseph had directed in Genesis 46:34. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)

### v. 4
The brothers explained they had come to sojourn because the famine in Canaan was severe and there was no pasture for their flocks. They asked to dwell in Goshen.

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The phrase "to sojourn in the land are we come" is described as an unconscious fulfillment of the ancient prophecy in Genesis 15:13 (that Abraham's descendants would be strangers in a land not theirs). They emphasized it was solely the extreme drought that caused them temporarily to vacate their own land. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Gill**: The brothers said nothing about wanting corn for themselves (they could buy that), only about pasture for their cattle. Canaan, being higher ground, was scorched and parched, while Goshen, lying lower near the Nile, still had grass even when the Nile did not overflow. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)
- **Matthew Henry** (summarised): The brothers honestly stated their purpose — it was only for a temporary stay, not permanent settlement. But "while man proposes, God disposes." (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_047.cfm)

### vv. 5–6
Pharaoh told Joseph to settle his father and brothers in the best of the land — Goshen. He also told Joseph to put any capable men among them in charge of Pharaoh's own livestock.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: This blessing of receiving "the best of the land" was because of Joseph. The whole family of Israel was blessed and received an inheritance because of Joseph. The offer to make them chief herdsmen over royal livestock assumes at least some of the brothers were competent at this work. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)
- **Gill**: "Men of activity" translates *chayil* — men strong in body and of great skill, diligence, and industry in managing flocks and herds. The office was like that of Doeg the Edomite, chief of Saul's herdsmen (1 Samuel 21:7). Gill adds that this shows Egyptians did not abstain from animals or universally despise shepherds — only foreign marauding ones. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)
- **Ellicott** connects this to the later need for capable herdsmen to manage the cattle Joseph would acquire from the people during the famine (see v. 16). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Wilkinson (the Egyptologist) thought Jacob's sons "may have asked and obtained a grant of land from the Egyptian monarch on condition of certain services being performed by themselves and their descendants." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)

### v. 7
Joseph brought in his father Jacob and presented him before Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.

- **Ellicott**: The presentation of Jacob was far more solemn than that of the brothers. Pharaoh looked on the brothers as the kin of his vizier, but Jacob had attained an age giving him great dignity — to an Egyptian, 120 was the utmost limit of longevity, and Jacob was 130. Pharaoh treats him with the greatest honour and twice accepts his blessing. "More must be meant by this than the usual salutation... Pharaoh probably bowed before Jacob as a saintly personage, and received a formal benediction." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Gill**: Jacob blessed Pharaoh not merely in a civil way but "in an authoritative way, as a prophet and patriarch, a man divinely inspired of God." The Targum of Jonathan records Jacob's prayer as: "May it be the pleasure of God that the waters of the Nile may be filled, and that the famine may remove from the world in thy days." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: This was not just the customary royal salutation like "May the king live forever!" (2 Samuel 16:16; Daniel 2:4), but — conscious of his dignity as a prophet of Jehovah — Jacob pronounced a heavenly benediction. Calvin is quoted: "This word does not denote a common and profane salutation, but the pious and holy prayer of a servant of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Dr. Constable (expository notes)**: Jacob's blessing of Pharaoh is "unusual since it implies that in one sense (i.e., as one of God's elect) Jacob was superior to Pharaoh. Pharaoh was a man of immense worldly power and influence. 'The lesser is blessed by the greater' (Hebrews 7:7)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-47.html)

### v. 8
Pharaoh asked Jacob, "How many years have you lived?" (Literally, "How many are the days of the years of thy life?")

- **Gill**: Dr. Lightfoot thought Pharaoh had never seen so old a man before — so grave a head and so grey a beard — and asked in admiration. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The question reflects the tender interest Pharaoh took in the aged patriarch's appearance. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)

### v. 9
Jacob replied that his years of pilgrimage were 130 — few and evil, not attaining to the years of his fathers.

- **Ellicott**: The Hebrew word means "sojournings," not "pilgrimage" in the modern sense. Jacob was not a religious pilgrim but a sojourner — Canaan was not the native land of his race. "Few and evil" — evil certainly: from deceiving his father onward, Jacob's life was filled with anxiety, care, and sorrow (Laban's injustice, fear of Esau, Dinah's dishonour, the slaughter at Shechem, Rachel's death, the loss of Joseph). They were "few" only in comparison with his fathers (Abraham 175, Isaac 180). Ellicott adds: "In Pharaoh's eyes Jacob had lived beyond the usual span of human existence; but to himself he seemed prematurely old." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Jacob understood his life as a pilgrimage — his real home was somewhere else (heaven). The statement "few and evil" was not pessimistic; Jacob recognized that his life as a man mostly unconcerned with spiritual things, and its length, did not compare to eternity or to his more godly ancestors. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)
- **Gill**: Jacob calls his life a "pilgrimage" as every good man's life is — they are not at home, but seeking a better, heavenly country. Jacob's life was literally a pilgrimage: he dwelt in Canaan, removed to Padan-aram, returned to Canaan (Succoth, Shechem, Hebron), and now Egypt. The "evil" refers to his many afflictions detailed by Gill at length. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Since Joseph was now 37 (Genesis 45:6), Joseph was born in Jacob's 91st year; since this was in the 14th year of Jacob's stay in Padan-aram (Genesis 30:25), Jacob was 77 when he left Beersheba after securing the blessing (Genesis 28:1). Jacob's life fell short of his ancestors in duration but greatly surpassed theirs in miseries. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Dr. Constable**: The comparison with his fathers' ages also "suggests that neither Abraham nor Isaac had experienced the difficulties and distresses that Jacob had during his lifetime." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-47.html)

### v. 10
Jacob blessed Pharaoh again and departed from his presence.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Pharaoh acknowledged Jacob was a man of God by accepting his blessing. In the Egyptian religion, Pharaoh himself was thought to be a god. Egyptians of that time considered Pharaoh as the human embodiment of Ra, the sun god. This means that it was remarkable that he allowed Israel to bestow a blessing on him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)
- **Gill**: Jacob blessed Pharaoh on departure as he had upon entering — wishing all happiness, giving thanks for the honour and favours shown. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)

### v. 11
Joseph settled his father and brothers in the land of Egypt, giving them property in the best part of the land — the district of Rameses — as Pharaoh commanded.

- **Ellicott**: Though the LXX takes "land of Rameses" as equivalent to Goshen, it was more probably a special district within it; Goshen was a vast territory. Raamses (Exodus 1:11) is the same word with different vowels. Whether a town already existed or was later built taking the district's name is uncertain. If a town existed at this period, it would have been a poor village of shepherds' huts; but later, under Rameses II, it became "the centre of a rich, fertile, and beautiful land, described as the abode of happiness." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Some (Michaelis, Rosenmüller) hold it was the specific district within Goshen where Jacob first settled; others (LXX, Keil, Hengstenberg, Kalisch) say it is Goshen itself, named proleptically from the town Rameses later built (Exodus 1:11). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Gill**: Joseph gave them houses to dwell in, lands to till, and pastures for their flocks. Gill includes an extensive geographical discussion, noting that "Rameses" may refer to the Heracleotic nome (modern Fioum), the best and most fruitful part of Egypt — the only part producing olives, wine, and fine fruits, confirmed by Strabo, Leo Africanus, and the traveller Vansleb. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)

### v. 12
Joseph provided his father, brothers, and all his father's household with food according to their families.

- **Ellicott**: The Hebrew word is *taf* — "according to the clan or body of dependants possessed by each one." Ellicott notes, "Dan, with his one child, would have been starved to death if the allowance for himself and his household had depended upon the number of his 'little ones,' which is the usual translation of this word in the Authorised Version." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The phrase is literally "to (or according to) the mouth of the little ones," meaning either in proportion to the size of their families (LXX, Keil, Kalisch, Murphy), or with the tenderness a parent shows to offspring (Murphy), or covering the whole body from greatest to least (Calvin). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Gill**: Joseph nourished them "like infants," putting bread as it were into their mouths with care and tenderness. "In this Joseph was an eminent type of Christ, who supplies the wants of his people." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)

### v. 13
There was no food in all that region; the famine was so severe that the lands of Egypt and Canaan were exhausted (literally "fainted" or "languished") by it.

- **Pulpit Commentary**: Three possible reasons for the insertion of this section at this point are suggested: (1) to exhibit the extreme urgency requiring Joseph's care for his family (Bush); (2) to show the greatness of the benefit conferred on Joseph's house (Baumgarten, Keil, Lange); (3) to foreshadow the political constitution later bestowed on the Israelites (Gerlach). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Gill**: The Hebrew word can mean "raged" — the inhabitants became furious, like madmen. Kimchi says they were at their wits' end. Gill marvels that they did not violently break open the storehouses; he credits God's restraining providence, Joseph's prudent fortification of granaries, and his mild address to the people. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)

### v. 14
Joseph collected all the money in Egypt and Canaan in exchange for grain and brought it into Pharaoh's palace (treasury).

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Joseph was not only a hard worker and a brilliant administrator, but he was also an honest worker. He did not cheat Pharaoh. As a loyal employee he brought the money into Pharaoh's house." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)
- **Gill**: Joseph gathered "all the money" — he did not personally collect it but gathered it as it was brought to him. He acted faithfully; the money belonged to Pharaoh, who had bought the corn, built storehouses, and kept men to manage the distribution. Gill defends Joseph against any charge of price-gouging: the people sold freely in plenty, and the higher price in famine was justified by the great expense of collection, preservation, and distribution. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The verb "gathered" (*laqat*) is used only here of collecting money; it usually signifies gathering things lying on the ground, such as ears of corn (Ruth 2:3), stones (Genesis 31:46), or manna (Exodus 16:14). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)

### v. 15
When the money from Egypt and Canaan was exhausted, all the Egyptians came to Joseph saying, "Give us food. Why should we die before your eyes? For our funds have run out!"

- **Gill**: This seems to have occurred at the end of the fifth or beginning of the sixth year of the famine. The Canaanites, not being Egyptians, could not presume to come asking for corn on such terms. The Egyptians appealed to Joseph's humanity — "why should we die in thy presence?" — knowing such an argument would work on his tender and generous mind. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)
- **Enduring Word**: Food was available, but at a price. Because the famine lasted seven years, eventually people ran out of money. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)

### vv. 16–17
Joseph told them to bring their livestock in exchange for food since their money was gone. They brought horses, flocks, herds, and donkeys, and Joseph fed them with bread in exchange for all their livestock throughout that year.

- **Ellicott**: This was a merciful arrangement. The people were in want of food and their land was incapable of cultivation as long as the Nile did not overflow. The arrangement delivered owners from a burden and saved a portion of the cattle for when they would be needed again for agriculture. This also explains why Pharaoh wanted competent men among Joseph's brothers as chief herdsmen — managing so many cattle in a time of dearth was a serious matter (cf. 1 Kings 18:5–6). The mention of **horses** is important for dating the dynasty — the horse was introduced by the Hyksos. The mention of **sheep** is also significant since they do not appear on the most ancient Egyptian monuments (though goats were indigenous). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: "The severity of these terms of sale and purchase was not so great as at first sight appears, since to a famishing people under-fed cattle and starving horses must have been comparatively worthless." The Hebrew verb for "fed them" literally means "led" — as a shepherd leads and cares for his flock (cf. Psalm 23:2; Isaiah 40:11). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: "This was not as harsh as it might sound. The famine meant that their cattle and horses were under-fed." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-47.html)

### v. 18
When that year ended, they came to him the second year and confessed they had nothing left except their bodies and their land — money gone, livestock now belonging to Joseph.

- **Pulpit Commentary**: "The second year" is not the second year of the famine, but the year following the one in which they had given up their cattle. The people spoke with frank openness. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Ellicott** concurs: this is the year after the cattle exchange, not the second year of the famine overall. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)

### v. 19
The people begged Joseph to purchase them and their land in exchange for food, so they would become Pharaoh's servants. They also asked for seed so the land would not become desolate.

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The people voluntarily proposed their own servitude. The request for seed shows they still looked forward to the famine's end and were willing to work. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Gill**: The people made this proposal themselves; Joseph did not force it upon them. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/genesis/47.htm)

### vv. 20–21
Joseph acquired all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh; every Egyptian sold his field because the famine was severe. The land became Pharaoh's, and Joseph reduced the people to servitude (or "removed them to cities") from one end of Egypt to the other.

- **Pulpit Commentary** (crucial textual note): The Hebrew verb in v. 21 does **not** mean "enslaved" (contra LXX and Vulgate). It means "he removed them" or "caused them to pass over" — transferring them from country districts to the cities where the grain was stored. This was a considerate and merciful arrangement for more efficiently supplying them with food (Calvin, Keil, Lange, Wordsworth). The notion that populations were swapped between cities to complete their subjugation (Jarchi, Grotius, Rosenmüller, Kalisch) is rejected. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Ellicott**: Joseph has been accused of reducing a free people to slavery, but "undoubtedly he did vastly increase the royal power; but from what we read of the vassalage under which the Egyptians lived to a multitude of petty sovereigns... an increase in the power of the king, so as to make it predominant, would be to their advantage." The removal to cities was most merciful — people needed to be near the stored food. Herodotus later computed the number of cities in the Nile Valley at 20,000. Also, people could not reside directly on their plots of ground because they were overflowed annually by the Nile. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: The text implies that originally in Egypt the people held absolute title to their land; each citizen was the legitimate owner of the land he cultivated. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-47.html)

### v. 22
Joseph did not acquire the priests' land, for they had a portion (of food) assigned to them by Pharaoh. They ate Pharaoh's rations, so they did not sell their land.

- **Ellicott**: Herodotus (ii. 37) confirms it was still Egyptian custom for priests to receive a daily allowance of cooked food. This usage probably began in Joseph's time, though here it is ascribed to the king himself, not Joseph. Greek accounts represent the king, the priests, and the warriors as the only landholders in Egypt. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The priests' portion was of food, not land (contra Lange, Kalisch). The provision came from Pharaoh, not Joseph — so Joseph must not be charged with extending a State allowance to an idolatrous priesthood. They did not need to alienate their lands because they had State aliment during the famine. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)

### vv. 23–24
Joseph told the people that since he had acquired them and their land for Pharaoh, he was giving them seed to sow. At harvest, they must give a fifth to Pharaoh and keep four-fifths for themselves — for seed, food, and their households and children.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: "Joseph wasn't unfair. He fed the people when they would have otherwise starved, and in return asked for one-fifth (20%) annually from the produce of the land. Many people today would be happy with only 20% in total taxes." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)
- **Ellicott**: The seed would be given only when the famine was nearly over; these arrangements seem completed shortly before the end of the seventh year. "A fifth part of the produce would be a very moderate rent, especially as there were no rates or taxes to be paid. The whole expenses of the State had to be defrayed from this rent." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: This verse is "a sufficient refutation of the oft-preferred charge that Joseph had despoiled the Egyptians of their liberties, and converted a free people into a horde of abject slaves. Slave-owners are not usually content with a tax of only twenty percent on the gross revenues of their estates." If the people could afford to part with a fifth in the years of plenty, they could pay the same as rent under improved agriculture with equal ease. The people themselves did not consider it harsh. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Dr. Constable**: The 20% tax "was not out of line with what was common in that day in the ancient Near East. Really it was small since the average was 33 and one third percent." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-47.html)

### vv. 25–26
The people responded, "You have saved our lives. We have found favour in our lord's eyes, and we will be Pharaoh's servants." Joseph established it as a law over Egypt (still in effect "to this day") that a fifth belongs to Pharaoh, excepting the priests' land.

- **Ellicott**: "The people were more than satisfied with Joseph's regulations; and if he had made them dependent upon the Pharaoh, apparently he had broken the yoke of the smaller lords, the hereditary princes of the districts into which Egypt was parcelled out; and they were more likely to be well-treated by the ruler of the whole land than by men of inferior rank." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: "That a sort of feudal service is here intended — the service of free laborers, not bondmen — we may learn from the relationship of the Israelites to God, which was formed after the plan of this Egyptian model" (Gerlach). The Pulpit Commentary adds an extensive note confirming the biblical account through the testimonies of Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, and Strabo — that the kings became lords paramount of the soil, only priests held free land, and the population occupied farms at a uniform rent of one-fifth. It contrasts Joseph's clemency with Mohammed Ali's 19th-century decree that made himself sole owner of all Egyptian lands, stripping even mosques and charities without exception. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: "Joseph wisely enacted a law which remained a statute in Egypt for many generations. Its principles were later incorporated into Israeli law." The 20% tax was an income tax on all citizens except priests. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-47.html)

### v. 27
Israel settled in Egypt, in Goshen. They acquired property there, became fruitful, and multiplied exceedingly.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Henry Morris calculated that the initial group of about 100 grew at just over 6% per year, yielding several million descendants by the time Israel left Egypt 430 years later. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: "This was the commencement of the promise" (Genesis 46:3 — God's promise to make Israel a great nation in Egypt). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Dr. Constable**: "Under Joseph's administration Israel prospered, in contrast to Egypt, and increased in number without suffering deprivation or loss of independence. The fulfillment of God's promise to increase the seed of the patriarchs was advancing." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-47.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: "God was moving according to His plan to develop the Chosen Family into the Chosen Nation." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-47.html)

### v. 28
Jacob lived in Egypt seventeen years; his total lifespan was 147 years.

- **Pulpit Commentary**: This breaks down as 77 years in Canaan, 20 years in Padan-aram, 33 years again in Canaan, and 17 years in Egypt — totalling 147. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: Jacob's life lasted 147 years. When he knew his death was near, he made Joseph take a solemn oath. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)
- **Dr. Constable**: "Jacob lived 17 years in the care of Joseph who, ironically, had spent the first 17 years of his life in Jacob's care (Genesis 37:2)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-47.html)

### v. 29
When Israel's time to die drew near, he called Joseph and asked him to put his hand under his thigh and swear to deal kindly and faithfully with him — not to bury him in Egypt.

- **Ellicott**: For seventeen years Jacob saw the growing prosperity of his race. Though not in immediate danger of death, he had a long-pondered wish and wanted his mind set at rest. His desire to be buried at Machpelah was natural: Jacob's "whole nature was a loving one, and strongly influenced by home and domestic feelings." At Machpelah lay Abraham (whom he had known as a boy), his beloved father and mother, and Leah (who had at last won his affections). "There, naturally, he too wished to lie among his own." The hand-under-thigh oath follows the pattern of Genesis 24:2. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Enduring Word (Guzik)**: The oath followed the pattern of the oath Abraham made his servant swear in Genesis 24:1–9. "Israel knew Egypt was not his home. He belonged in the land promised to him and his descendants. He clearly believed and understood that he was the inheritor of Abraham's covenant." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)
- **Matthew Henry**: Jacob resolved to be buried in Canaan "not from mere humour, because Canaan was the land of his nativity, but in faith, because it was the land of promise... and because it was a type of heaven, that better country which he that said these things declared plainly that he was in expectation of" (Hebrews 11:14). He had Joseph sworn to give him satisfaction in his dying minutes: "Nothing will better help to make a death-bed easy than the certain prospect of a rest in Canaan after death." (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_047.cfm)

### v. 30
Jacob asked to be carried out of Egypt and buried with his fathers in their burial place. Joseph answered, "I will do as you have requested."

- **Pulpit Commentary**: The request, while due partly to the natural human instinct to be buried in ancestral graves, "was inspired by the clear faith that Canaan was the true inheritance of Israel, and that, though now obtaining a temporary refuge in Egypt, his descendants would eventually return to the land of promise as their permanent abode." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary**: "This was the testimony of Jacob's conviction that Israel would one day return to the land, to take up their rightful and permanent possession of it." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-47.html)

### v. 31
Jacob said, "Swear to me." Joseph swore, and Israel bowed in worship at the head of his bed.

- **Major text-critical note (Ellicott):** The LXX, followed by the Epistle to the Hebrews (11:21) and the Syriac, reads "on the top of his **staff**" rather than "on the head of his **bed**." The Hebrew word without vowels (*mittah* / *matteh*) can mean either. The Masoretic vowel-pointing (added later) gives "bed," but the points, while representing an ancient tradition, "are nevertheless not of final authority." Ellicott nevertheless judges the Authorised Version rendering "the most satisfactory. It was scarcely worth mentioning that Jacob bowed before Joseph, leaning on his staff; but the picture of the aged patriarch leaning back upon his bed, content and happy in his son's promise, and giving thanks to God for the peace of his approaching end, is one full of pathos and dignity." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: Though many eminent authorities support "bed" (Chaldee paraphrase, Symmachus, Vulgate, Calvin, Delitzsch, Keil, Kalisch), the reading "staff" has weight because (1) it is adopted by the writer to the Hebrews (Hebrews 11:21), (2) the Hebrew words for staff and bed differ only in the punctuation, and (3) leaning on a staff was quite as suitable to Jacob's circumstances as bowing on his bed's head. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)
- **Matthew Henry**: "Israel bowed himself upon the bed's head, yielding himself, as it were, to the stroke of death ('Now let it come, and it shall be welcome'), or worshipping God, as it is explained, Hebrews 11:21, giving God thanks for all his favours, and particularly for this, that Joseph was ready... to give him the satisfaction he desired concerning his burial. Thus those that go down to the dust should, with humble thankfulness, bow before God, the God of their mercies, Psalm 22:29." (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_047.cfm)

## Denominational Perspectives

In my research, I did not find significant **doctrinal disputes** among Protestant traditions over this chapter. Most traditions read Genesis 47 in substantially the same way — as historical narrative demonstrating Joseph's wise administration, God's providential care for Israel, and Jacob's faith in the covenant promises. However, notes of emphasis do differ:

- **Reformed (Calvin, cited in Ligonier/devotional and Pulpit):** Emphasises God's sovereignty. Jacob, who wrestled God to a standstill, cannot by his own strength go to Egypt; God must guide him providentially. "Truly, the Lord's will is accomplished by His Spirit, not our might or power (Zech. 4:6)." (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/move-canaan) Calvin insists Jacob's blessing of Pharaoh was "not a common and profane salutation, but the pious and holy prayer of a servant of God." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)

- **Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Emphasises Joseph's wise, godly administration and God's unfolding plan to develop the "Chosen Family into the Chosen Nation." Joseph's 20% tax is presented as a model of equitable governance later incorporated into Israeli law. The voluntary servitude of the Egyptians is read straightforwardly as indentured service, not chattel slavery. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/genesis-47.html)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik):** Draws practical spiritual applications: Jacob's "pilgrimage" perspective models the believer's true home in heaven; Pharaoh's acceptance of Jacob's blessing (despite being considered the god Ra) shows that even the powerful recognise genuine spiritual authority; Joseph's honest administration models workplace integrity. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-47/)

- **Matthew Henry (broadly Evangelical/Puritan):** Interprets Jacob's burial request typologically — Canaan as "a type of heaven, that better country which he that said these things declared plainly that he was in expectation of" (Hebrews 11:14). The deathbed scene becomes a model for dying in faith. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_047.cfm)

- **Methodist/Wesleyan, Lutheran, and Anglican** specific commentaries on this chapter were not returned in the searches, though the older Anglican voice of Ellicott is well represented above.

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (text-critical)

- **NET Bible notes** could not be fetched due to tool limits. However, the key scholarly issue in this chapter — whether v. 31 reads "bed" or "staff" — is thoroughly discussed by Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary (see v. 31 above). The LXX reading "staff" is followed by Hebrews 11:21 in the New Testament, giving it apostolic authority while the Masoretic "bed" has strong traditional support.

- **Ellicott** also provides the significant historical note about **horses** in v. 17: "The horse was introduced by the Hyksos, according to Lenormant... and the first representation of one is drawing the war-chariot of the king who expelled them." This bears on dating Joseph to the Hyksos period. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/genesis/47.htm)

- **Pulpit Commentary** cites Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, and Strabo to confirm that after Joseph's time the Egyptian kings became lords paramount of the soil, priests alone held free land, and the population occupied farms at a uniform rent of one-fifth — corroborating the biblical account from extra-biblical sources. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-47.html)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

- No results were retrieved from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search/fetch limits. The LXX reading of v. 31 ("staff" rather than "bed"), followed by Hebrews 11:21, is the reading used in Orthodox liturgical tradition. The Catholic Haydock Commentary and Orthodox patristic readings would likely emphasise Jacob's faith as commended in Hebrews 11 and the typological significance of Joseph as a type of Christ providing bread to the world — but specific pages could not be accessed.
